stem: For x > 0, what is the derivative of f(x) = 4/√x?

rationales.A: This adds 1 to the exponent (−1/2 + 1 = 1/2) instead of subtracting 1, giving 4(−1/2)x^(1/2) = −2√x. Subtracting 1 gives the exponent −3/2, so f′(x) = −2/x^(3/2).
rationales.B: This gets the exponent −3/2 right but multiplies by −1 instead of by the exponent −1/2, giving 4(−1)x^(−3/2) = −4/x^(3/2). The power rule multiplies by the exponent: 4(−1/2) = −2, so f′(x) = −2/x^(3/2).
rationales.D: This loses the negative sign from the exponent −1/2. The power rule gives 4(−1/2)x^(−3/2) = −2/x^(3/2).

stem: An ellipse is given by x² − 2x + 4y² − 8y = 11. At exactly one point (a, b) with a > 0 and b > 0, the tangent line to the ellipse is vertical. Which of the following is that point?

rationales.A: This point is on the ellipse (9 − 6 + 4(4 + 2√3) − 8 − 8√3 = 11), but there dy/dx = (1 − 3)/(4√3) = −1/(2√3), so the tangent is neither vertical nor horizontal. Lying on the curve is not enough; y − 1 must be 0.
rationales.B: Implicit differentiation gives 2x − 2 + 8y · dy/dx − 8 · dy/dx = 0, so dy/dx = (1 − x)/(4(y − 1)). The tangent is vertical where the denominator is 0 and the numerator is not, i.e. y = 1. Substituting into the curve gives x² − 2x + 4 − 8 = 11, so x² − 2x − 15 = 0 and x = 5 or x = −3. With a > 0, the point is (5, 1).
rationales.C: This point is on the ellipse (1 − 2 + 36 − 24 = 11), but there dy/dx = (1 − 1)/(4 · 2) = 0, so the tangent is horizontal, not vertical. The vertical condition is a zero denominator, y − 1 = 0.
rationales.D: This point has y = 1, the vertical-tangent condition, but is not on the ellipse: 1 − 2 + 4 − 8 = −5, not 11. The condition must be combined with the curve's equation, which gives x² − 2x − 15 = 0, so x = 5 for a > 0.

stem: Which of the following correctly identifies the rules needed to differentiate f(x) = e^(x²)/(x + 3)?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Quotient Rule only, since e^(x²) is its own derivative

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chain Rule only, with x + 3 as the inner function

choices.label: C
choices.text: Product Rule only, writing e^(x²)(x + 3)⁻¹ as a product

choices.label: D
choices.text: Quotient Rule, with the Chain Rule for e^(x²)

rationales.A: The derivative of e^(x²) is 2x e^(x²), not e^(x²), because the exponent x² is a composite inner function. The quotient rule alone leaves out the factor 2x.
rationales.B: f is a ratio of two functions, not a function evaluated at x + 3, so the chain rule alone cannot differentiate it. The division also needs the quotient rule (or a product rule on a rewritten form), together with the chain rule for e^(x²).
rationales.C: Even after rewriting as a product, the factor e^(x²) is a composite function whose derivative is 2x e^(x²), which needs the chain rule. The product rule alone is not enough.
rationales.D: f is a quotient of e^(x²) and x + 3. The numerator e^(x²) is a composite function, so its derivative uses the chain rule: 2x e^(x²). Thus f′(x) = (2x e^(x²)(x + 3) − e^(x²))/(x + 3)².
